settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The evaluation context is SimpleEvaluationContext (lines 180-190), not StandardEvaluationContext, which by design restricts type references, constructors, and bean references.

setPropertyValue first calls isWritableProperty and throws NotWritablePropertyException for paths not resolvable against the target type, so arbitrary expression text that does not map to a real property path does not reach evaluation.
The unit test rejectsExpressionContainingTypeExpression asserts that a T(...) type expression is rejected, surfaced as SpelEvaluationException wrapped in NotWritablePropertyException.

The changelog records DATACMNS-1264 'MapDataBinder should reject type expressions in SpEL expressions' as addressed, and the checked-out tree already contains the corresponding test, i.e. the fix is present in this snapshot.
No BeanFactoryResolver or StandardEvaluationContext is wired into this binder, so bean/type access primitives are absent from this path.
candidates.description: MapDataBinder.MapPropertyAccessor.setPropertyValue validates the incoming property name only with isWritableProperty/getPropertyPath (a PropertyPath.from check for the parameter type) and then passes the raw, user-controlled property name to PARSER.parseExpression(propertyName), evaluating it with expression.setValue(context, value) against a SimpleEvaluationContext. The parser is constructed with SpelParserConfiguration(false, true), enabling auto-grow of collections/maps during evaluation, and PropertyTraversingMapAccessor.read auto-creates nested Map/Collection entries. The property-name allow-list (PropertyPath) and the SpEL grammar operate on the same user string but differ, so expression constructs embedded in a name (indexers, nested navigation, operators) may be parsed and evaluated rather than being strictly limited to the dotted-property form. Root cause: untrusted input used as a SpEL expression source. I could not establish a concrete security-relevant effect from the allowed source spans; this is a residual concern, not a confirmed exploit.
missing_evidence: No runtime or exploit demonstration that a specific property name produces a security-relevant effect (for example SSRF, file access, or data corruption) under SimpleEvaluationContext.
Not verified which released versions ship without the DATACMNS-1264 fix; the checked-out tree already contains the fix and its tests.
No analysis of whether auto-grow (SpelParserConfiguration(false, true)) plus nested map creation can be abused for resource exhaustion; no depth/size limit was located or quantified.
No inspection of how the resulting Map is consumed downstream, which would be needed to establish impact.
ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver was not read in this review, so the request-to-binder data flow is inferred rather than traced from source.
preconditions: Spring Data web support is enabled and a handler method argument is resolved by ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver so that MapDataBinder binds a request-derived property/value map.
An attacker can influence the property names (and values) reaching the binder, e.g. request parameter names.
The application-defined parameter type exposes writable properties matching the supplied path prefixes so that isWritableProperty passes.
candidates.title: MapDataBinder evaluates attacker-influenced property names as SpEL expressions
